live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL (Kimsuky): a North Korea-linked espionage group with many names, phishing lures and layered malware
next.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL, widely tracked as Kimsuky, is assessed by several vendors to be North Korea-linked. Reports describe spearphishing of South Korean targets, multi-stage scripts and cloud-based data theft.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as NICKEL KIMBALL. The catalogue lists many other names, including Kimsuky, APT43, Velvet Chollima, Black Banshee, Emerald Sleet, THALLIUM and TA427.
Tools the catalogue links to the actor include BabyShark, ReconShark, KONNI, KimJongRAT, FastFire, FastSpy and FireViewer.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes a command server it analysed to Kimsuky (APT43, Velvet Chollima, Black Banshee) and calls it a DPRK actor, with high confidence.

Genians Security Center assesses with moderate confidence that a 2026 campaign was the work of Kimsuky, which it calls a North Korea-linked group. It says no single decisive piece of evidence was found and that imitation by a third party cannot be ruled out.
Sekoia and Kudelski Security note that some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster with several branches, such as TA406 and TA408. They also say vendors divide and name clusters differently.
The same report identifies cyberespionage as the primary objective of the threat clusters it describes, a group that includes Kimsuky.
Attribution is not always clean. Some research firms detected malware in an Iranian-linked campaign as Kimsuky or Lazarus, while ClearSky attributed it to a subgroup of Charming Kitten.

Lookout found that a North Korea-linked Android spyware campaign, which it attributed to APT37 with medium confidence, also had ties to infrastructure used by APT43. Lookout notes that North Korean groups share infrastructure, targeting and techniques, which makes attribution harder.
Genians describes a 2026 campaign that approached South Korean policy and security professionals.
Breakglass Intelligence reports phishing lures aimed at South Korean users of Naver, including tax-themed lures.
In 2022, ESRC analysed a malicious Word file disguised as a customer-center guide from Klip, a digital asset wallet service. ESRC linked it to Thallium, also known as Kimsuky.
Genians describes reply-based spearphishing in which the sender posed as an aide to a National Assembly member. The victim got an archive holding a shortcut file disguised as a document.

In that campaign, later stages ran in memory, set up persistence with a scheduled task and used built-in Windows tools. A public note service served as an extra control channel, and the operator swapped its contents to change tools.

Genians reports that stolen data went to cloud services such as Dropbox, MEGA and free web hosting. The tools it saw included XenoRAT variants and a Node.js-based remote access tool it named NodeLinkRAT.

Breakglass Intelligence describes a three-stage chain that starts from a compiled help file disguised as API documentation. The stages do reconnaissance and persistence, bridge to PowerShell, then run a keylogger with clipboard monitoring and timed exfiltration.
The same report maps about 79 domains across five IP addresses, using Korean and US hosting providers and free dynamic DNS services.

The 2022 ESRC analysis found a macro-laden document that asked users to enable content. The macro dropped an XML file that ran and tried to reach a command server, which could not be reached at the time.
Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that it detected APT43 actors using multiple public AI tools. It says the purpose of that access is not clear.
Genians dates the 2026 campaign's activity from June to October 2026. It places the spearphishing of a seminar attendee between September 12 and 18, 2026.
Breakglass Intelligence says a researcher submitted the help file to MalwareBazaar in April 2026. The report was published on 2026-04-11.
Lookout's KoSpy Android spyware, disguised as utility apps, had samples from March 2022 to March 2024. Lookout says the apps were removed from Google Play.
Be wary of unexpected replies and attachments, even from a sender who seems to hold an official role. Shortcut files and help files inside archives deserve extra suspicion.
Watch for odd traffic to cloud storage and note-sharing services, and treat attribution to one named group as provisional.
